evidence.claim: Putin approved instructions requiring the government to create a special procedure to assess families whose members lost jobs after March 1, 2022, expand access to social support for families with children whose income fell, add support for the unemployed, index pensions and social benefits, raise the minimum wage and subsistence minimum, and allocate federal funds for regional support and infrastructure.
evidence.title: Instructions following a meeting on socioeconomic support for regions
evidence.excerpt: Putin approved instructions requiring the government to create a special procedure to assess families whose members lost jobs after March 1, 2022, expand access to social support for families with children whose income fell, add support for the unemployed, index pensions and social benefits, raise the minimum wage and subsistence minimum, and allocate federal funds for regional support and infrastructure.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Direct presidential instructions on a dated 2022 policy package; the page states the specific actions and implementation deadlines.
evidence.period_fit: Directly within 2022 and tied to Putin's formal authority.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct: Putin approved the instructions and tasked the government; implementation depended on ministries and regional authorities.
contrary_evidence: The order is reactive crisis management during war and sanctions, not proof of durable welfare improvement.
Benefits were mediated by government and regional implementation.

evidence.claim: Rosstat said 2022 poverty was 9.8% (14.3 million people), down from 11.0% in 2021, and that targeted state support in 2022 reduced income differentiation; the correction was based on household survey and administrative data.
evidence.title: Росстат уточнил данные о численности населения с доходами ниже границы бедности в 2022 году
evidence.excerpt: Rosstat said 2022 poverty was 9.8% (14.3 million people), down from 11.0% in 2021, and that targeted state support in 2022 reduced income differentiation; the correction was based on household survey and administrative data.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official statistical revision with named methodology and sample size, but still a state source and not independent of policy claims.
evidence.period_fit: Covers the target year 2022, though published in 2023 after revision.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Partial: the statistic reflects state social support under Putin, but also wages, prices, and measurement revisions.
contrary_evidence: Official framing may over-credit policy and understate wartime inflation or regional disparities.
Poverty remained substantial despite the decline.

evidence.claim: Rosstat said the 8-17 child cash benefit introduced on April 1, 2022 covered 3.7 million families and more than 5.5 million children during 2022, while social payments and targeted social programs were a main driver of lower poverty.
evidence.title: Росстат представляет информацию о границе бедности в IV квартале 2022 года
evidence.excerpt: Rosstat said the 8-17 child cash benefit introduced on April 1, 2022 covered 3.7 million families and more than 5.5 million children during 2022, while social payments and targeted social programs were a main driver of lower poverty.
evidence.source_locator: poverty section / social support bullet points
evidence.source_confidence_reason: The page gives explicit beneficiary counts and links them to social payments, but it is an official statistical communication and should be corroborated.
evidence.period_fit: Directly covers 2022 implementation and beneficiary reach.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Partial to direct: the benefit expansion was a 2022 state policy under Putin, but delivery and take-up depend on administrative execution.
contrary_evidence: Coverage counts do not show adequacy, equality, or who was excluded.
The same source still shows millions below the poverty line.

evidence.claim: UNICEF's Russia SDG dashboard shows that 100% of children were covered by social protection floors/systems in 2020, while 12% of children were below the national poverty line in 2020 and 0% were in extreme poverty in 2022.
evidence.title: Child-Related SDG Progress Assessment for Russian Federation
evidence.excerpt: UNICEF's Russia SDG dashboard shows that 100% of children were covered by social protection floors/systems in 2020, while 12% of children were below the national poverty line in 2020 and 0% were in extreme poverty in 2022.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: UNICEF compiles internationally comparable indicator data, but this page is a dashboard with lagged indicator years and not ruler-specific causal attribution.
evidence.period_fit: Lagged indicators around the target year; useful as baseline/context rather than direct 2022 policy proof.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Mostly inherited/system-level context; it does not isolate Putin's 2022 marginal contribution.
contrary_evidence: The social protection coverage indicator is from 2020 rather than 2022.
Dashboard indicators do not prove service quality or inclusion for all groups.

evidence.claim: UNICEF's dashboard reports that 97% of the population used basic drinking water services in 2022, 89% used basic sanitation, 76% used safely managed drinking water, 61% used safely managed sanitation, and open defecation was 0%.
evidence.title: Child-Related SDG Progress Assessment for Russian Federation
evidence.excerpt: UNICEF's dashboard reports that 97% of the population used basic drinking water services in 2022, 89% used basic sanitation, 76% used safely managed drinking water, 61% used safely managed sanitation, and open defecation was 0%.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: UNICEF compiles standardized global data; however the indicators are summary statistics, not direct evidence of Putin's choices.
evidence.period_fit: 2022 indicator values, though not direct policy causation.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Mostly inherited/system-level baseline; limited direct attribution to Putin absent a specific 2022 service-delivery reform.
contrary_evidence: Coverage is unevenly distributed across indicator types and still below universal safe service levels.
This is outcome data, not evidence that Putin improved access in 2022.

evidence.claim: UNICEF's dashboard reports that Russian Federation had 97% DTP3 coverage in 2022, 100% skilled birth attendance in 2020, and an under-five mortality rate of 5 per 1,000 live births in 2021.
evidence.title: Child-Related SDG Progress Assessment for Russian Federation
evidence.excerpt: UNICEF's dashboard reports that Russian Federation had 97% DTP3 coverage in 2022, 100% skilled birth attendance in 2020, and an under-five mortality rate of 5 per 1,000 live births in 2021.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Global indicator dashboard with lagged years; useful for baseline but not direct ruler attribution.
evidence.period_fit: Near-target-year health outcome indicators, but not a 2022 policy act.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Mostly inherited/system-level context; limited evidence of marginal improvement attributable to Putin in 2022.
contrary_evidence: Health outcomes lag policy and may reflect earlier investments rather than 2022 actions.
Indicator coverage does not show regional or class disparities.

evidence.claim: WHO says Russia has universal health coverage with free care in state and municipal facilities, but quality and availability vary widely by region; the basic package is set federally while territorial packages can differ.
evidence.title: Russian Federation health system information
evidence.publisher: WHO European Observatory on Health Systems and Policies
evidence.excerpt: WHO says Russia has universal health coverage with free care in state and municipal facilities, but quality and availability vary widely by region; the basic package is set federally while territorial packages can differ.
evidence.source_locator: country profile / health system overview lines 150-151
evidence.source_confidence_reason: WHO/Observatory synthesis is authoritative on system design, though it describes structure rather than 2022 performance.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Mostly inherited institutional context; it does not by itself show Putin strengthened or weakened service delivery in 2022.
contrary_evidence: Universal coverage does not guarantee equal quality or access.
Regional variation limits direct inference about nationwide welfare gains.

evidence.claim: WHO's country data says life expectancy at birth in Russia improved by 4.86 years from 65.2 in 2000 to 70.0 in 2021, and healthy life expectancy improved by 4.23 years over the same period.
evidence.title: Russian Federation
evidence.excerpt: WHO's country data says life expectancy at birth in Russia improved by 4.86 years from 65.2 in 2000 to 70.0 in 2021, and healthy life expectancy improved by 4.23 years over the same period.
evidence.source_locator: life expectancy / healthy life expectancy country overview
evidence.source_confidence_reason: WHO country data are a standard source for health outcomes, but the figures are lagged and not a 2022 policy attribution on their own.
evidence.period_fit: Latest available health trajectory close to 2022; not direct 2022 policymaking evidence.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Inherited long-run trajectory more than Putin-specific 2022 action; use cautiously as baseline and trend context.
contrary_evidence: The page does not isolate 2022 or Putin's specific contribution.
Health gains may reflect earlier decades and non-Putin factors.

evidence.claim: Reuters reported that Russian consumer demand contracted at its fastest pace in seven years in 2022, real disposable incomes fell 1%, retail sales dropped 6.7%, and unemployment stayed low at 3.7%, while top officials linked the labor-market strain to mobilization and sanctions.
evidence.title: Russia's 2022 economic fall seen in lower incomes, slumping consumer demand
evidence.excerpt: Reuters reported that Russian consumer demand contracted at its fastest pace in seven years in 2022, real disposable incomes fell 1%, retail sales dropped 6.7%, and unemployment stayed low at 3.7%, while top officials linked the labor-market strain to mobilization and sanctions.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters is a strong wire-service source, and the passage cites Rosstat data with concrete 2022 household outcomes.
evidence.period_fit: Directly about 2022 household outcomes, published early 2023.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Strong on negative attribution to Putin's invasion and mobilization decisions; some components also reflect sanctions and preexisting labor-market conditions.
contrary_evidence: Low unemployment is a partial positive counterpoint.
The article notes the economy withstood sanctions better than first expected.

evidence.claim: Reuters reported that Russia's 2022 budget deficit reached 2.3% of GDP, below a prewar surplus target, because of the Ukraine war's burden on state finances and a shift toward security and defence spending.
evidence.title: Russia says budget deficit hit 2.3% of GDP in 2022
evidence.excerpt: Reuters reported that Russia's 2022 budget deficit reached 2.3% of GDP, below a prewar surplus target, because of the Ukraine war's burden on state finances and a shift toward security and defence spending.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters quotes the finance minister and states the budget consequence clearly.
evidence.period_fit: Directly about 2022 fiscal outcomes and wartime spending choices.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Strong: the deficit and reallocation are consequences of Putin's war and budget priorities, though the precise fiscal line is implemented by the finance ministry.
contrary_evidence: A deficit is not by itself proof of social welfare failure; some spending was countercyclical support.
Oil revenues and domestic borrowing softened the immediate shock.

evidence.claim: The World Bank said Russian poverty could rise to 14.1% in 2020 without fully compensatory measures, and that existing social protection programs announced in January, March, and April 2020 could partly compensate for crisis impacts on families with children, the unemployed, and SMEs.
evidence.title: COVID-19 (Coronavirus) Policy Response to Protecting the Poorest and Most Vulnerable in Russia
evidence.excerpt: The World Bank said Russian poverty could rise to 14.1% in 2020 without fully compensatory measures, and that existing social protection programs announced in January, March, and April 2020 could partly compensate for crisis impacts on families with children, the unemployed, and SMEs.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: World Bank analysis is methodologically stronger than political advocacy, but it is a forecast and predates the target year.
evidence.period_fit: Pre-2022 baseline context on crisis response capacity and welfare architecture.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Mostly baseline and institutional context; it shows preexisting social protection channels rather than Putin-specific 2022 improvement.
contrary_evidence: It is a 2020 forecast, not a 2022 outcome.
The measures are described as partial compensation rather than a solution.

evidence.claim: The World Bank said schoolchildren in Russia were at risk of learning losses of up to six months, that poor and under-represented students were more likely to suffer dropout or lower qualifications, and that Russia moved to distance-learning measures and digital platforms.
evidence.title: COVID-19 (Coronavirus) Policy Response to Addressing Learning Gaps and Inequalities in Russia
evidence.excerpt: The World Bank said schoolchildren in Russia were at risk of learning losses of up to six months, that poor and under-represented students were more likely to suffer dropout or lower qualifications, and that Russia moved to distance-learning measures and digital platforms.
evidence.source_locator: challenges / what Russia has done to confront these challenges
evidence.source_confidence_reason: World Bank country brief is credible for baseline and response description, but it is pre-2022 context and not direct evidence of 2022 outcomes.
evidence.period_fit: Baseline context only; pre-target-year education/distribution conditions.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Mostly inherited context and pandemic response architecture; limited Putin-specific 2022 attribution.
contrary_evidence: It is about COVID-era disruption, not 2022 social policy.
The brief is about risks and mitigation, not demonstrated outcome improvement.

unresolved_gaps: Direct evidence on command-and-control discipline, custody, accident-prevention, and other nuclear safety procedures in 2022 is thin.
Direct evidence on expert governance and risk institutions is weak relative to the rhetoric and escalation evidence.
The package needs better household and distribution evidence, not just macro stabilization and state-budget outcomes.
Direct evidence that appointments and institutions translated into durable productivity investment is still thin.
Direct 2022 delivery evidence for health, education, housing, and food security inside Russia remains thin.
Implementation and take-up by region and group are not well documented.
Direct documentary proof of Putin's personal beneficial ownership, asset control, or hidden conflicts remains limited.
The appointment and accountability map is still too thin for a fully rounded honesty judgment.
Direct 2022 implementation metrics for procurement, output, and battlefield effectiveness remain thin.
The package still needs a cleaner separation between frantic adaptation, temporary stabilization, and genuinely effective goal advancement.
